# Mixture Modelling (a.k.a. modelling heterogeneity)

In mixture model, we account for heterogeneity in the data by assuming that there is not "one single" data generating process, but actually K of them. Therefore, we expect to find K different subpopulations (or _clusters_) in our data, and that each subpopulation is homogeneous: it is suitably modeled by a density, typically from a parametric family.

In its most general form, let $f_1(\cdot), \ldots, f_K(\cdot)$ be $K$ probability density functions over a space $(\mathbb{Y}, \mathcal{Y})$, $\mathbf{w} = (w_1, \ldots, w_K)$ a vector in the $(K-1)$-dimensional simplex; a mixture model assumes the following likelihood

\begin{equation}
    y_1, \ldots, y_n \mid \mathbf{w}, \{f_j\}_{j=1}^K \overset{iid}{\sim} f(y) := \sum_{j=1}^K w_j f_j(y)
    \tag{1}
\end{equation}

We refer to the $f_j$'s as the _components_ of the mixture

The connection to clustering is made more explicit by introducing "cluster assignment" variables $c_i$, $i=1, \ldots, n$ such that
$$
    P(c_i = h \mid \mathbf{w}) = w_h
$$

Then, the mixture likelihood can be restated as the following hierarchical model

\begin{equation}
    \begin{aligned}
        y_i \mid c_i = h, \{f_j\}_{j=1}^K & \overset{ind}{\sim} f_h \\
        P(c_i = h \mid \mathbf{w}) &= w_h
    \end{aligned}
    \tag{2}
\end{equation}

Usually, $\{f_j\}_{j=1}^K$ belong to the same parametric family (e.g., the normal distribution), and differ only for the specific values of the parameters (e.g., every component has a different mean/variance). But this might not always be the case.

# Generate data from Mixture Models

In order to understand how mixture models works, a useful exercise is to generate a synthetic dataset from a mixture of Gaussian distributions.

Suppose, for example, that we want to generate 10000 samples from the following mixture density:
\begin{equation}
  f(y) = 0.3\ \mathcal{N}(y \mid -5, 2) + 0.5\ \mathcal{N}(y \mid 0,1) + 0.2\ \mathcal{N}(y \mid 5,3),
  \tag{3}
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{N}(\cdot \mid \mu, \sigma^2)$ is the probability density function (pdf) of a Gaussian distribution with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ evaluated in $\cdot$.  

We can follow the hierarchical specification in (2) to construct the algorithm:
\begin{itemize}
  \item for $i = 1,\dots,n$
  \begin{itemize}
    \item sample the cluster allocation $c_i \sim \text{Categorical}(0.3, 0.5, 0.2)$
    \item if $c_i = 1$, sample $y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(y \mid -5, 2)$, if $c_i = 2$, sample $y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(y \mid 0,            1)$, else sample $y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(y \mid 5,3)$
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

```{r}
# Define weights, means and standard deviations of the mixture
weights <- c(0.3, 0.5, 0.2)
means <- c(-5.0, 0.0, 5.0)
std_devs <- c(2.0, 1.0, 3.0) ^ 0.5
```

```{r}
# Function that generates n i.i.d. samples from a mixture of Gaussian distributions
gaussian_mixture_rng <- function(n, weights, means, std_devs) {
  clus_allocs <- sample(length(weights), n, replace = TRUE, prob = weights)
  data_rng <- rnorm(n, mean = means[clus_allocs], sd = std_devs[clus_allocs])
  return(data_rng)
}

# Generate 10000 samples
n <- 10000
data_rng <- gaussian_mixture_rng(n, weights, means, std_devs)

hist(data_rng, probability = TRUE, breaks = 50, col = rgb(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, alpha = 0.7), border = "white", main = "", xlab = "")
```

# Galaxies in the Shapley Supercluster

The `shapley` dataset (available in te `R` package `spatstat`) is a point pattern dataset recording the sky positions of 4215 galaxies in the Shapley Supercluster.

This dataset comes from a survey by [Drinkwater et al (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1071/AS03057) of the Shapley Supercluster, one of the most massive concentrations of galaxies in the local universe. The data give the sky positions of 4215 galaxies observed using the FLAIR-II spectrograph on the UK Schmidt Telescope (UKST). They were kindly provided by Dr Michael Drinkwater through the Centre for Astrostatistics at Penn State University.

Sky positions are given using the coordinates Right Ascension (degrees from 0 to 360) and Declination (degrees from -90 to 90).

The point pattern has three mark variables:
- **Mag**: Galaxy magnitude (a negative logarithmic measure of visible brightness);
- **V**: Recession velocity (km/sec) inferred from redshift, with corrections applied.
- **SigV**:Estimated standard error for V.

We aim to cluster the galaxies in the Shapley supercluster according to their recession velocities (in $10^{-3}\ km / s$). The `shapley.csv` file attached stores such quantity in proper format.


```{r, eval = TRUE}
# Parse dataset
data <- read.csv("shapley.csv")
# Subsample - Take 1000 observations
data <- data$V[sample(nrow(data), 1000)]
# Plot the data
hist(data, main = "", xlab = "V", breaks = 20)
```

# Exercise 2: Posterior computation with Mixture Models
Consider the `shapley.csv` dataset we have introduced in the previous section:

We can model the data using a mixture of $H = 7$ gaussian distributions.

\begin{equation*}
    y_1, \ldots, y_n \mid \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{\mu}, \mathbf{\sigma}^2 \overset{iid}{\sim} \sum_{h=1}^{7} w_j \mathcal{N}(\mu_j, \sigma^2_j)
\end{equation*}

The vector $\mathbf{w}$ represent the probability that a subject belongs to one of the 7 groups. A natural marginal prior choice is therefore a Dirichlet($\mathbf{\alpha}$) distribution. With no prior information available, we can assume that $\mathbf{\alpha} = (1,\dots,1)$.

```{r}
# Helper function
r_dirichlet <- function(alpha) {
  y <- rgamma(length(alpha), shape = alpha, rate = 1)
  return(y / sum(y))
}

run_one_gibbs <- function(data, cluster_allocs, uniq_vals, weights) {
  # Set n_clus
  n_clus <- length(weights)
  # Update Unique Values
  for (h in seq_len(n_clus)) {
    clusdata <- data[cluster_allocs == h]
    if (length(clusdata) == 0) {
      uniq_vals[h, ] <- sample_uniq_vals_prior()
    } else {
      uniq_vals[h, ] <- sample_uniq_vals_fullcond(clusdata)
    }
  }
  # Update cluster allocs
  cluster_allocs <- update_cluster_allocs(data, weights, uniq_vals)
  # Update weights
  weights <- update_weights(cluster_allocs, n_clus)
  
  return(list(cluster_allocs = cluster_allocs, uniq_vals = uniq_vals, weights = weights))
}

run_mcmc <- function(data, niter = 7500, nburn = 2500, thin = 5) {
  # Set number of components
  H <- 7
  # Initialize chain
  cluster_allocs <- sample(H, length(data), replace = TRUE, prob = rep(1/H, H))
  weights <- rep(1/H, H)
  init_vars # <- initialize the variance sampling from the prior
  init_means # <- initialize the mean sampling from the prior
  uniq_vals <- cbind(init_means, init_vars)
  # Prepare output
  allocs_out <- list()
  uniq_vals_out <- list()
  weights_out <- list()
  # Sampler for loop
  pb <- txtProgressBar(min = 1, max = niter, style = 3)
  for (i in seq_len(niter)) {
    setTxtProgressBar(pb, i)
    # Sample
    res <- run_one_gibbs(data, cluster_allocs, uniq_vals, weights)
    cluster_allocs <- res$cluster_allocs
    uniq_vals <- res$uniq_vals
    weights <- res$weights
    # Save state
    if (i > nburn && i %% thin == 0) {
      allocs_out[[length(allocs_out) + 1]] <- cluster_allocs
      uniq_vals_out[[length(uniq_vals_out) + 1]] <- uniq_vals
      weights_out[[length(weights_out) + 1]] <- weights
    }
  }
  close(pb)
  # Return chain
  return(list(allocs_out = allocs_out, uniq_vals_out = uniq_vals_out, weights_out = weights_out))
}
```

# Exercise 3: Posterior inference with Mixture Models

Mixture models are subject to the so called "label switching", which causes non-identifiability for all the parameters.

Label switching means that permuting the "labels" {1, 2, ..., K} of the cluster yields the same exact likelihood.
Hence, it does not make sense to talk about "first", "second" and "third" cluster.
Moreover, also interpretation of the cluster parameters is tricky: we cannot say that, given the total number of iterations S,

$$
    \hat{\mu}_h = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^S \mu^{(s)}_h
$$

is an estimate of parameter $\mu_h$, the mean of the $h$-th cluster. Also, it does not make sense to take averages of the cluster allocation labels.

There are several ways to solve this non-identifiability issue, we will focus here on a decision-theoretic approach.


3.1) Implement a function that finds the clustering, among the ones visited in the MCMC chain, that minimizes Binder's loss function. The Binder loss is defined, for each post-burnin sample $s$, as

$$
    \text{Loss}^{(s)} = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n (\mathbb I [c^{(s)}_i = c^{(s)}_j] - p_{ij})^2
$$
where $p_{ij}$ is the posterior probability that observations $i$ and $j$ belong to the same cluster and $c_i^{(s)}$ the cluster label for unit $i$ in iteration $s$.

Note that $p_{ij}$ can be easily estimated from the MCMC chains!

3.2) Given the estimated clustering $\mathbf{c}^*$, estimate the parameters in each cluster. Let $c^*_h$ denote the index-set of the $h$--th cluster (e.g., $c^*_1 = \{1, 3, 10\}$, $c^*_2 = \{0, 2, 4, 5, 6\}$ ...). Then
$$
    \hat \mu_h = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^S \frac{1}{\# c^*_h} \sum_{i \in c^*_h} \mu^{(s)}_{c_{i}^{(s)}}
$$
where $\mu^{(s)}_\ell$ is the mean of the $\ell$--th cluster at the $s$--th MCMC iteration.

Similarly for the variance $\hat \sigma_h^2$.

3.3) Comment on the posterior inference obtained

```{r}
unique_vals_given_clus <- function(unique_vals_chain, clus_alloc_chain, best_clus) {
  c_allocs <- do.call(rbind, clus_alloc_chain)
  uniq_vals <- simplify2array(unique_vals_chain)
  means <- uniq_vals[, , 1]
  variances <- uniq_vals[, , 2]
  out <- list()
  
  # TODO: fill out
  unique_best <- unique(best_clus)
  for (h in seq_along(unique_best)) {
    clus_val <- unique_best[h]
    data_idx <- which(best_clus == clus_val)
    uniq_vals_idx <- c_allocs[, data_idx, drop = FALSE] # -> Matrix [n_iter X n_data_in_clus]
    means_by_iter <- matrix(0, nrow = nrow(c_allocs), ncol = length(data_idx))
    vars_by_iter <- matrix(0, nrow = nrow(c_allocs), ncol = length(data_idx))
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(c_allocs))) {
      means_by_iter[i, ] <- NA
      vars_by_iter[i, ] <- NA
    }

    avg_mean_by_iter <- NA
    avg_var_by_iter <- NA
    
    muhat <- NA
    varhat <- NA
    
    out[[length(out) + 1]] <- c(muhat, varhat)
  }
  
  return(out)
}
```
